newsitem.title: UK: Brazil 97/98 coffee output seen at 26 mln bags - EIU.
newsitem.headline: Brazil 97/98 coffee output seen at 26 mln bags - EIU.

text.p: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) on Tuesday maintained its forecast for Brazilian coffee production at 26 million bags for 1997/98, unchanged from the current season.

"With no frost damage to trees this winter and much better ground moisture levels than in some recent years, a harvest about on par with this season's is still indicated for 1997/98 (April/March)," the EIU said in its latest quarterly world commodity forecast.
Brazil would have an exportable production of 17.5 million bags in 1997/98, 500,000 bags more than in 1996/97, it said.
The EIU said it had slightly trimmed its exportable output forecasts largely due to downward adjustments in Colombia.
"Lower prices to growers, reduced spending on inputs and coffee borer damage are taking a heavier than expected toll, underlined by the frequent cuts in estimates of the 1995/96 harvest," it said.
But an upturn in production was expected for 1996/97, as larger crops were foreseen for central America and Mexico and Asian and African outputs were also expected to rise.
The EIU forecast world exportable coffee production at 76.1 million bags in 1996/97, rising to 77.5 million in 1997/98 -- both sharply higher than the 65.8 million turned out in 1995/96.
Its consumption estimate was for 74.1 million bags for 1996/97 and 75.6 million for 1997/98, after 73.4 million in 1995/96.
"Encouraged by falling retail prices...consumption is... slightly better than first predicted, especially in southern and eastern Europe," the report said.
"Our revised forecasts still show the coffee market moving into surplus in the coming two seasons, but by less than previously expected," it said.

The report added that the new figures suggested scope for only a fairly modest stock rebuilding after three years of particularly sharp declines. Most of the forecast stock increase was expected in robustas.

"A precipitate drop in prices can thus be ruled out, with the picture ahead remaining one of continuing gradual decline from the peak touched in mid-1994 in the wake of that year's frosts in Brazil's producing zone," the report said.
